study.title: 1 Corinthians 7 - marriage, loosening, vocation and faithfulness in the Lord
study.overview: In this chapter, Paul answers church questions about marriage, separation, remarriage, celibacy and Christian life in different social conditions. The axis of argumentation is not a devaluation of marriage, nor a universal imposition of soltisirice, but the defense that every believer lives faithfully to Christ in the situation in which he was called. The chapter holds together two principles: marriage is good and legitimate, and undivided dedication to the Lord is also a good, especially in times of pressure and distress. Paul also deals with believing and unbelieving spouses, circumcised persons or not, of slaves and free, showing that faith does not automatically erase external conditions, but redefines the way to live them before God.

outline.title: Marriage as protection against immorality and recognition of the gift of continence
outline.explanation: Paul begins by answering church questions about sexual relations and marriage. He states that because of sexual immorality, marriage is the legitimate path to sexual exercise within fidelity. At the same time, he emphasizes that abstinence can be good for some, but it is not a universal commandment; there is a diversity of gifts, and whoever has no self-control should marry, because it is better to marry than to live consumed by desire.

outline.title: Marital fidelity, coexistence with unbelievers and permanence in the vocation
outline.explanation: Here Paul presents instructions for married marriages: not seeking separation, and, if there is separation, to remain without marriage or seek reconciliation. When a spouse is disbelievers, if he consents to live together, the believer should not abandon him, because coexistence is seen as an occasion of holy and peaceful influence, although he does not guarantee the salvation of the other. Then Paul generalizes the principle: each one must remain in the condition in which he was called, without treating conversion as an automatic reason to change social or religious status.

outline.title: Virginity, haste of the present time and freedom to marry in the Lord
outline.explanation: Paul proceeds to advise virgins without appealing to a commandment directly from the Lord, but as a reliable opinion because of the present need. He does not condemn marriage, but argues that the present crisis and the brevity of time recommend simple life, detachment from earthly anxieties and service to the Lord without distraction. At the close, he states that the widow is free to marry again, as long as she is in the Lord, although she considers it happier to remain as it is; this assessment is presented as an apostolic opinion associated with her consciousness of acting under the Spirit of God.

study.context: The chapter answers questions the church of Corinth sent by letter. The notes provided indicate that the community was dealing with practical doubts about marriage, separation and Christian life amid pressures and afflictions of the present time. It also appears the background that there was strong sexual immorality, which helps explain why Paul values marriage as a legitimate remedy for many. The notes also note that the question about marriage was relevant both for Gentiles and for converts coming from Judaism, including in situations of unions with unbelievers.
study.theology: The theology of the chapter unites creation, holiness and vocation. Marriage is honored as a good and faithful institution, but it is not absolute; fidelity to Christ can be lived both in marriage and in loosening. Paul sees sexuality as something that must be ordained by holiness and mutual responsibility, not selfishness. The clause on the unbeliever who consents to live together suggests that the presence of the believer may have a sanctifying effect in the home, without this means automatic salvation of the other or the children. The broader principle is that God's call redefines the believer's identity: circumcision or uncircumcision, slavery or social freedom, the civil state or widowhood do not determine the value before God. What is ultimately worth is to obey the commandments of God and live as a servant of Christ, bought for a high price. Paul also values peace as a pastoral goal and recognizes that the brevity of present history must produce detachment from temporal circumstances.

scholarViews.insight: Paul recommends looseness as an ideal because of his conviction that Christians belong entirely to Christ, but admits that marriage is not sin.
Marriage is presented as a remedy against sexual immorality; therefore it is better to marry than to burn in desire.
Paul treats the situation of the married believers with unbelievers and guides that the converted spouse does not abandon the other if he consents to remain together.

questions: How does this chapter correct the idea that looseness is always more spiritual than marriage, or that marriage is always the only mature choice?
How does the instruction to remain in the condition in which it was called helps the church to avoid hasty changes motivated by guilt, status or social pressure?
How can faith live in the home and work peacefully, without confusing sanctifying influence with control over the other's decision?
study.practice: Evaluate your current vocation before Christ: if you are single, married, widowed, employed, free, or live under limitations, try to serve the Lord with integrity where you are. Married persons should cultivate fidelity, dialogue and prayer, without using spirituality as an excuse to neglect the spouse. Singles and widowers can be considered serenly if their condition favors greater dedication to the Lord, without guilt or haste. In any state, concrete application is this: not to organize your life by fear, comparison or anxiety, but by the call of God, for peace and obedience to the commandments.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided make it clear that some of Paul's instructions are apostolic opinion and not commandment directly from the Lord, especially in the verses about virgins and widowhood. There is also limitation as to the expression about the person sanctified by the unbelieving spouse: the notes suggest influence in the home, but do not authorize automatic salvation. In addition, Adam Clarke's reading of the virgin's case at the end of the chapter may include the possibility of a parent responsible for the girl, but this is not explicitly resolved by the notes; therefore, the study avoids defining this detail as a certain fact.
